extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and drafting patent specifications under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (and pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph), covering the separate requirements of written description, enablement, and best mode, with special considerations for computer‑implemented inventions and means‑plus‑function claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must include a written description of the invention: "the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: ensure claimed scope does not overreach inventor's contribution. Key points: must describe the invention so a person of ordinary skill understands the inventor actually invented the claimed subject matter; applies to all claims including original claims; no special rule for supporting a genus by species—support depends on state of the art and breadth. Examples/anti‑patterns: merely indicating a result or using generic boundaries without describing species is insufficient (see Regents of Univ. of Cal. v. Eli Lilly; Ariad; LizardTech). Functional/generic claim language often raises written description issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must set forth the manner and process of making and using the invention in "such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make and use the same" — i.e., teach how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is separate from written description. Examiner should evaluate enablement against the claim as a whole (everything within claim scope must be enabled). The specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but must supply information necessary to enable the novel aspects. Examples: inability to enable the full breadth of a broad claim can render it invalid (MagSil, Sitrick). Omission of specific starting materials or process conditions may require undue experimentation. See also guidance on undue experimentation factors (Wands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Mode Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must "set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor ... of carrying out the invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two factual inquiries: (1) subjective — did the inventor know of a best mode at filing; (2) objective — if so, was it disclosed in sufficient detail to allow one skilled in the art to practice it. Only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is considered; to sustain a best mode rejection evidence must show the quality of disclosure is so poor as to effectively result in concealment. For software, disclosure of the functions of the software usually satisfies best mode (flow charts or source code not required). See In re Gay; Spectra‑Physics; Fonar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue Experimentation Factors (Wands test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether undue experimentation is required (i.e., enablement), weigh the Wands factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of one of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; (8) quantity of experimentation needed to make or use the invention. The undue experimentation determination is reached by weighing all these considerations together (In re Wands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's Burden to Establish a Reasonable Basis for Enablement Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Before making an enablement rejection, USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning whether the disclosure enables a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the examiner advances a reasonable basis for questioning enablement, the applicant must rebut and factually demonstrate that the disclosure is sufficient. Cases: In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle; In re Scarbrough. Examiners should analyze what the claim recites and what subject matter it encompasses as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Commensurate in Scope With the Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of enablement provided by the specification — i.e., the specification must enable the full scope of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee choosing broad claim language risks losing claims that cannot be enabled across their full scope. If the specification enables only a narrower scope, broader claims may be invalid for lack of enablement (MagSil; Convolve). Examiners should consider whether the specification teaches how to make and use embodiments across the claim's full range (see also Sitrick example where video/game teachings did not enable movies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description for Computer‑Implemented Functional Claims (algorithm/structure disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer‑implemented functional claim limitations, the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding computer and algorithmic structure (the necessary steps and/or flowcharts) so that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm may be expressed as mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or other understandable terms that provide sufficient structure. It is not enough that one skilled in the art could write a program to achieve the function; the specification must explain how the inventor intended the function to be performed. If the specification fails to disclose the computer and algorithm in sufficient detail, a written description rejection must be made. See Finisar; Vasudevan; Ariad; MPEP §§2163, 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑(or Step‑)‑Plus‑Function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) Corresponding Structure Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre‑AIA sixth paragraph), the specification must provide corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the entire claimed function; absent such disclosure, the applicant has failed to particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a means/step‑plus‑function limitation lacks sufficient corresponding structure in the specification, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (second paragraph) must be made in addition to any written description rejection. See In re Donaldson; MPEP §2181. Examiner should check for adequate disclosure of structure/materials/acts that perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus‑Species Support for Broad (Genus) Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of a species does not automatically support a claim to a broader genus; whether a genus is supported depends on the state of the art and the nature and breadth of the genus. Adequate written description of a genus requires more than a generic statement of boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must convey to one skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the genus (Hynix). Disclosure of some species can support a genus if it reasonably conveys possession of the broader subject matter, but disclosure of only a single embodiment often does not (LizardTech). Anti‑patterns include claiming a broad genus based on one method/embodiment without evidence the inventor conceived other species achieving the genus result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of Functional or Generic Claim Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims defined solely by desired results or by functional language, without describing how the function is performed, often fail the written description (and/or enablement) requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly acute for genus claims that use functional language to define boundaries: the functional claim may claim a desired result without describing species that achieve it. For software, simply restating a function in the claim without explaining the algorithm/steps/procedure is insufficient. Examiner should look for disclosure of how the function is achieved, not merely the statement of the goal (Ariad; LizardTech; MPEP §§2163.02, 2181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on Knowledge of One Skilled in the Art Is Limited
rubrics_metrics.description: While the specification need not disclose what is well known in the art, the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information necessary to enable the novel aspects of the claimed invention when that information is not known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of supplementation: well known information may be omitted, but omission is not a substitute for a basic enabling disclosure of novel aspects. Cases: Genentech; ALZA; Auto. Technologies. Omission of only minor details may be acceptable, but lack of disclosure of any specific starting materials or conditions when needed can render the specification non‑enabled.
